vulnerabilities.title: Tax Swap Accounting Bug Allows Permanent Loss of Project Tax Tokens
vulnerabilities.description: The _swapTax function incorrectly reduces projectTaxPendingSwap when performing a partial swap (when swapBalance < contractBalance), but the reduction formula is mathematically flawed. It subtracts (projectTaxPendingSwap * swapBalance) / contractBalance, which assumes the tax tokens in the contract balance are proportional to the pending swap amount. However, the contract balance includes both tax tokens and potentially other tokens (e.g., from failed swaps or deposits), making the ratio invalid. This causes projectTaxPendingSwap to be under-reduced, leaving tokens unclaimed in the contract while the pending counter is too high. Subsequent swaps further compound the error, and the distributeTaxTokens function can only distribute the (now incorrect) pending amount, permanently locking the excess tax tokens in the contract.

vulnerabilities.title: Tax Swap Accounting Inconsistency Allows Theft of Project Tax Funds
vulnerabilities.description: The _swapTax function incorrectly reduces projectTaxPendingSwap based on the ratio of swapBalance to contractBalance, but this ratio is computed using the total contract balance (including non-tax tokens) rather than the actual tax balance. This allows an attacker to manipulate the tax accounting by transferring non-tax tokens to the contract, causing the protocol to undercount pending tax and permanently lose project tax funds.

vulnerabilities.title: Automatic ETH Processing via receive() Enables Double Funding of Tax Tokens
vulnerabilities.description: The contract's receive() function accepts ETH without any checks, and combined with the _autoSwap mechanism, allows an attacker to trigger tax token swaps by sending ETH to the contract. This causes the contract to incorrectly treat ETH deposits as tax accumulation, leading to double funding: the attacker receives both the swapped pair tokens AND retains their original ETH deposit.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds + Double Funding Risk

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted Tax Rate Reduction Enables Fee Manipulation
vulnerabilities.description: The setProjectTaxRates function allows the owner to reduce tax rates but does not prevent them from being reduced to zero after taxes have been collected. This enables an attacker to manipulate the tax collection mechanism by first accumulating tax tokens, then reducing tax rates to zero, and finally withdrawing the accumulated tax tokens without paying any further taxes. This breaks the economic invariant that taxes are meant to be collected on every transaction, allowing the owner to effectively steal accumulated tax funds.

vulnerabilities.title: Auto-Swap Threshold Calculation Uses Total Supply Instead of Circulating Supply
vulnerabilities.description: The _autoSwap function calculates the swap threshold using _totalSupply, which includes tokens held in the vault and liquidity pool. However, only circulating tokens should be used to determine when to trigger auto-swaps. This causes auto-swaps to trigger prematurely when the total supply is large but circulating supply is small, leading to unnecessary swaps and potential loss of tax revenue due to slippage. The calculation should use circulating supply (totalSupply - vaultBalance - liquidityPoolBalance) to accurately reflect the tax-generating activity.

vulnerabilities.title: Tax Pending Swap Calculation in _swapTax is Vulnerable to Rounding Errors and Underflow
vulnerabilities.description: The _swapTax function reduces projectTaxPendingSwap using integer division: (projectTaxPendingSwap * swapBalance_) / contractBalance_. This can result in rounding down, causing the pending tax to be undercounted. If the swapBalance_ is not a perfect divisor of contractBalance_, the remainder is lost. Over multiple swaps, this leads to permanent loss of tax tokens. For example, with 1000 tax tokens and 999 pending, a swap of 999 tokens results in 999 * 999 / 1000 = 998, leaving 1 token unaccounted for. This error accumulates over time, leading to significant fund loss.

vulnerabilities.title: Liquidity Pool Access Control Bypass via Direct Transfer to Uniswap Pair
vulnerabilities.description: The _pretaxValidationAndLimits function prevents transfers to the uniswapV2Pair before fundingDate, but only if the sender is not the contract itself. However, an attacker can call transferFrom with the contract as the 'from' address and the uniswapV2Pair as the 'to' address, bypassing the check since the sender is not the contract. This allows an attacker to manipulate the initial liquidity price by transferring tokens directly to the pair before the owner adds liquidity, distorting the token's initial market value.

vulnerabilities.title: distributeTaxTokens Allows Double-Spending of Tax Tokens
vulnerabilities.description: The distributeTaxTokens function transfers projectTaxPendingSwap to the recipient and sets it to zero. However, if an attacker triggers an auto-swap immediately after calling distributeTaxTokens, the auto-swap logic will still attempt to reduce projectTaxPendingSwap based on the previously transferred amount, even though it was already zeroed out. This creates a race condition where the same tax tokens can be claimed twice: once via distributeTaxTokens and once via auto-swap, leading to double-spending of tax revenue.

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted Minting Beyond Cap via Constructor and External Mint Function
Unrestricted Minting Allows Infinite Token Supply Despite Capped Constructor
vulnerabilities.description: The VirtualToken contract inherits ERC20Capped, which enforces a supply cap of 1e9 VIRTUAL (1 billion tokens). However, the mint() function, which is only restricted by onlyOwner, does not check whether the total supply after minting exceeds the cap. This allows the owner to mint beyond the declared cap, effectively nullifying the cap protection. The cap is only enforced in ERC20Capped._mint() when called internally, but since the owner can call mint() directly and the cap check is not re-enforced in the override context, the cap is bypassed. This leads to inflation beyond the protocol's stated limit, diluting all existing token holders.

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted Minting Allows Infinite Token Supply Bypassing Cap
vulnerabilities.description: The VirtualToken contract inherits ERC20Capped, which enforces a maximum supply of 1e9 VIRTUAL (1,000,000,000 * 10^18 wei). However, the mint() function calls ERC20._mint(), which bypasses the cap enforcement in ERC20Capped. ERC20Capped's _mint() override checks the cap only when called via the public mint() function, but _mint() internally (as used here) skips the cap check. This allows the owner to mint any arbitrary amount of tokens beyond the cap, effectively nullifying the cap protection. Since token supply is a core economic variable used in fee distribution, reward calculations, and liquidity weighting, this creates a systemic risk of inflation and dilution. An attacker with owner privileges can mint unlimited tokens, diluting all other holders and potentially collapsing tokenomics.

vulnerabilities.title: No Receive Function or Deposit Handling - Protocol Cannot Accept Native Currency
vulnerabilities.description: The VirtualToken contract is an ERC20 token that does not implement a receive() or fallback() function, and has no mechanism to accept or process native currency (ETH). This is not a vulnerability in the traditional sense of fund theft, but it creates a critical operational failure: users cannot deposit ETH into the protocol to exchange for VIRTUAL tokens, and any ETH sent to the contract is permanently lost. This breaks the fundamental economic model of a token that is intended to be used within a DeFi protocol requiring native currency deposits. The contract is designed to be minted by the owner, but there is no on-ramp for users to acquire tokens via ETH, rendering the token non-functional in any real-world DeFi context.

vulnerabilities.title: Tax Pending Swap Accounting Vulnerability Due to Integer Division Truncation
vulnerabilities.description: The _swapTax function reduces projectTaxPendingSwap using integer division (projectTaxPendingSwap * swapBalance_ / contractBalance_), which truncates fractional values. This causes permanent loss of tax tokens over time as the pending swap counter is under-decreased, leading to funds being permanently locked in the contract. The truncation occurs because Solidity integer division rounds down, and the loss accumulates with each swap.

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call in _swapTax Leads to Incomplete Tax Distribution
vulnerabilities.description: The _swapTax function commits state changes (projectTaxPendingSwap reduction) only after the external swap call, but if the swap fails, the state change is still applied due to the try/catch swallowing the revert. This means tax tokens are deducted from pendingSwap even when the swap to pairToken fails, resulting in permanent loss of tax revenue without any corresponding ETH/WETH distribution.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - State Commitment Timing

vulnerabilities.title: Auto-Swap Eligibility Bypass via Router Address Spoofing
vulnerabilities.description: The _eligibleForSwap function checks !isLiquidityPool(from_) and from_ != address(_uniswapRouter), but does not validate that the sender is not a malicious contract impersonating the router. An attacker can deploy a contract with the same address as _uniswapRouter (via CREATE2) and trigger auto-swaps without being blocked, potentially draining tax balances by triggering multiple swaps in one transaction.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - Authorization Context Binding

vulnerabilities.title: distributeTaxTokens Allows Double-Spending of Tax Tokens via Reentrancy
vulnerabilities.description: The distributeTaxTokens function transfers projectTaxPendingSwap to projectTaxRecipient without reentrancy protection. If projectTaxRecipient is a malicious contract, it can reenter distributeTaxTokens and withdraw the same pendingSwap multiple times before projectTaxPendingSwap is set to zero, leading to double-spending of tax tokens.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - Operation Reversal Completeness

vulnerabilities.title: Unvalidated PairToken in _createPair Leads to ABI Incompatibility Risk
vulnerabilities.description: The contract assumes pairToken is a valid ERC20 token, but does not validate that it implements the expected ERC20 interface (e.g., balanceOf, transfer). If pairToken is a non-compliant token (e.g., a fork with different function signatures), the addInitialLiquidity and _swapTax functions will revert during external calls, locking liquidity and tax tokens permanently.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: External Integration Integrity - Interface Definition Compatibility

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call in executeApplication Leads to Reentrancy and Fund Loss
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function commits state (sets application.status to Executed and zeroed withdrawableAmount) before executing external calls to create token, DAO, veToken, NFT, and TBA. If any of these external calls revert (e.g., due to insufficient gas, malicious implementation, or front-running), the state remains permanently committed, preventing the application from being withdrawn or re-executed, while the applicationThreshold deposit is irreversibly consumed. This creates a scenario where user funds are locked permanently due to a failed external dependency.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing User Protection in executeApplication: No Minimum Output Guarantee for Token Creation
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function creates a new token and liquidity pool using external calls, but provides no mechanism for the user (proposer) to specify minimum acceptable outputs (e.g., minimum LP tokens, minimum token supply, minimum veToken stake). If the token implementation is malicious or the Uniswap router is manipulated, the LP pool could be created with 0 liquidity or a negligible amount, while the user's entire applicationThreshold deposit is locked into the pool. The user has no recourse to cancel or reject the execution, leading to permanent loss of funds.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Missing User Control Over Execution Outcomes

vulnerabilities.title: Validation of Application Status Occurs After State Mutation in withdraw
vulnerabilities.description: In the withdraw function, the application.status is checked and then immediately mutated to Withdrawn before the token transfer. However, if the IERC20.safeTransfer reverts (e.g., due to a malicious token or insufficient balance), the status is already set to Withdrawn, and the withdrawableAmount is zeroed. This prevents the proposer from retrying the withdrawal, even though the funds were not transferred. Validation occurs after state change, violating Pattern 2 and locking user funds.

vulnerabilities.title: State Synchronization Failure in _executeApplication: VirtualId Used Before Assignment
vulnerabilities.description: In _executeApplication, the virtualId is read from IAgentNft(nft).nextVirtualId() and used in the mint call, but the application.virtualId is only assigned after the mint call. If the mint call reverts (e.g., due to NFT contract logic or gas limit), the application.virtualId remains 0, but the NFT was already minted at that virtualId. This creates an orphaned NFT with no record in the application mapping, breaking the protocol's state consistency and potentially allowing the same virtualId to be reused or exploited.

vulnerabilities.title: Unverified External Contract Assumptions in _createNewAgentToken
vulnerabilities.description: The _createNewAgentToken function assumes that the cloned token implementation's initialize function will always create exactly one liquidity pool at index 0, which is then used in _executeApplication. However, the token implementation is user-controlled via setImplementations and may be malicious or misconfigured. If the token implementation creates no liquidity pools or creates them at a different index, the subsequent IAgentToken(token).liquidityPools()[0] call will revert, causing the entire executeApplication to fail. But since state was already committed (status=Executed, funds transferred), the user's deposit is permanently lost. This violates Pattern 8 (External System Assumptions).

vulnerabilities.title: Reentrancy Vulnerability in withdraw and executeApplication Due to No Reentrancy Guard on External Calls
vulnerabilities.description: Although the noReentrant modifier is applied to withdraw and executeApplication, it only protects against direct reentrancy into the same function. However, during the execution of external calls (e.g., IERC20.safeTransfer, Clones.clone, IAgentNft.mint, IERC6551Registry.createAccount), a malicious token or NFT contract can reenter the AgentFactoryV3 contract via a callback. For example, a malicious token could call withdraw(id) again during the safeTransfer in executeApplication, leading to double withdrawal of the same applicationThreshold. The noReentrant flag is set after the modifier check, but external calls can still reenter other functions if they are not guarded.

vulnerabilities.title: Incorrect Unit Usage in executeBondingCurveApplication: Token Supply Parameters Mismatch
vulnerabilities.description: The executeBondingCurveApplication function constructs _tokenSupplyParams using abi.encode(totalSupply, lpSupply, totalSupply - lpSupply, ...) but the setTokenSupplyParams function expects the 3rd parameter to be vaultSupply. In executeBondingCurveApplication, the 3rd parameter is totalSupply - lpSupply, which is intended to be the vault supply, but this assumes totalSupply = lpSupply + vaultSupply. If the caller passes totalSupply = 1000, lpSupply = 300, then vaultSupply = 700. But if the token implementation expects vaultSupply to be the actual vault allocation (e.g., 700), and instead receives 700 as totalSupply - lpSupply, it may be correct. However, if the token implementation expects vaultSupply to be a percentage or a different unit (e.g., basis points), this causes a unit mismatch. The function assumes the token implementation uses the same parameter semantics as setTokenSupplyParams, but this is not enforced. This could lead to incorrect token distribution, e.g., if vaultSupply is interpreted as a multiplier or percentage, causing massive inflation or locking of tokens.

vulnerabilities.title: Front-Running Risk in TBA Creation via Predictable Address with CREATE2
vulnerabilities.description: The TBA (Token Bound Account) is created using IERC6551Registry.createAccount with a tbaSalt and chainId. Since CREATE2 uses a deterministic address calculation based on salt, implementation, and deployer, an attacker can precompute the TBA address before the application is executed. The attacker can then deploy a malicious contract at that address before the legitimate createAccount call. When AgentFactoryV3 calls createAccount, it will return the attacker's pre-deployed contract instead of a fresh clone. The attacker's contract can then control the TBA, intercept all future interactions, steal NFTs, or drain assets. This violates Pattern 8 (External System Assumptions) and Pattern 6 (State Synchronization).

vulnerabilities.title: State Inconsistency in Application Status and WithdrawableAmount During executeApplication
vulnerabilities.description: The _executeApplication function sets application.status to Executed and resets withdrawableAmount to 0 before executing any external calls. However, if any of the subsequent external calls (e.g., _createNewAgentToken, _createNewDAO, IAgentNft.mint, IERC6551Registry.createAccount, or IAgentVeToken.stake) revert due to external failures (e.g., insufficient gas, invalid implementation, or reentrancy), the application state is permanently corrupted: the withdrawableAmount is consumed (transferred to the token contract) and the status is set to Executed, but the agent components are never created. This prevents the proposer from ever withdrawing the funds again, as the application is no longer Active, and the funds are locked in the newly created (but possibly invalid) token contract. This is a critical state inconsistency where state commitment (status update and fund transfer) occurs before external operations complete, violating the principle of 'commit after success'.

vulnerabilities.title: Incorrect Unit Handling in executeBondingCurveApplication Returns Value
vulnerabilities.description: The executeBondingCurveApplication function returns the token address via IAgentNft(nft).virtualInfo(application.virtualId).token. However, IAgentNft is an interface that likely expects virtualInfo to return a struct containing multiple fields (token, dao, proposer, etc.). The return type of executeBondingCurveApplication is declared as address, but if IAgentNft.virtualInfo returns a struct, the ABI will decode the first field (token) as an address — which is correct — but the caller expects only the token address. The issue is not in the return type per se, but in the assumption that IAgentNft.virtualInfo returns a struct with token as the first field. If the external IAgentNft contract is a fork or has a different struct ordering (e.g., token is not the first field), the returned address will be garbage. This leads to the caller (e.g., bonding curve contract) using an incorrect token address for subsequent operations, potentially locking funds or transferring them to a wrong address. This is a unit/semantic mismatch: the function is expected to return a token address, but the return value is derived from an external contract whose interface structure is not verified.

vulnerabilities.title: Reentrancy Risk in _executeApplication via External Calls Before State Finalization
vulnerabilities.description: The _executeApplication function performs multiple external calls (Clones.clone, IAgentToken.initialize, IAgentVeToken.stake, IERC6551Registry.createAccount, IAgentNft.mint) after setting application.status = Executed and transferring funds to the token contract. If any of these external contracts (e.g., the cloned token contract) have reentrant logic (e.g., in their initialize function), they can re-enter AgentFactoryV3 and call executeApplication again on the same or another application ID. Since application.status is already Executed, the reentrant call will revert due to the require(status == Active), but the initial call has already transferred the withdrawableAmount to the token contract. This means the attacker can trigger multiple executions of the same application by exploiting reentrancy in a malicious token implementation, causing the same applicationThreshold to be transferred multiple times to different token contracts, effectively draining the factory's assetToken balance. The reentrancy guard (locked flag) only prevents direct reentrancy into the same function call stack, but not reentrancy via external contract callbacks.

vulnerabilities.title: Unverified External Interface Compatibility for IAgentNft and IERC6551Registry
vulnerabilities.description: The contract assumes that IAgentNft.nft().mint() and IERC6551Registry.createAccount() behave as expected. However, if the external IAgentNft contract is a fork (e.g., from a different protocol) that has changed the order of parameters in mint() or requires additional parameters (e.g., metadata URI, royalty info), the ABI encoding will fail or corrupt the call. Similarly, IERC6551Registry.createAccount expects specific parameters (implementation, salt, chainId, tokenContract, tokenId). If the registry is a fork that requires a different order (e.g., tokenId before tokenContract), the TBA will be created at a wrong address or revert. This leads to a broken TBA, which may prevent users from interacting with their virtual personas. Since the factory does not validate the external contract's interface structure or behavior, a malicious or incompatible implementation can cause permanent failure of agent creation, locking funds in unaccessible TBAs or tokens. This is a critical dependency risk with no interface verification.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing Validation of tbaImplementation in proposeAgent and initFromBondingCurve
vulnerabilities.description: The proposeAgent and initFromBondingCurve functions accept tbaImplementation as a user-provided address with no validation. An attacker can pass a malicious address (e.g., a contract that reverts on createAccount or has no createAccount function). When executeApplication is called, IERC6551Registry.createAccount will revert, causing the entire application execution to fail. However, the withdrawableAmount has already been transferred to the token contract (in _executeApplication), and the status is set to Executed. The proposer cannot withdraw because the application is Executed, and the TBA creation failed — so the funds are permanently locked. There is no fallback or recovery mechanism. This is a critical input validation failure: user-controlled addresses used in critical external interactions must be validated for code existence and function compatibility.

vulnerabilities.title: Incorrect Use of block.timestamp + maturityDuration in veToken Initialization
vulnerabilities.description: The _createNewAgentVeToken function uses block.timestamp + maturityDuration to set the end time for staking. However, if the transaction is mined with a delay (e.g., due to congestion), block.timestamp may be significantly ahead of the proposer's expectation. More critically, if the maturityDuration is set to 0 or very small, the veToken becomes immediately unstakable. But the bigger issue is that the maturityDuration is set by the admin and is global. This means all agents inherit the same maturity duration. If an attacker sets maturityDuration to 1 second via setMaturityDuration (only admin can do this), then every new agent's veToken becomes immediately unstakable. This breaks the entire staking mechanism for all future agents. The financial impact is that users who stake their LP tokens will immediately be able to unstake, destroying the locking mechanism and undermining the veToken's purpose. This is a global state variable that, if manipulated, breaks protocol invariants for all users.

vulnerabilities.title: Funds Locked in _vault if NFT Minting Fails After Token and LP Creation
vulnerabilities.description: In _executeApplication, the NFT is minted to _vault after the token and LP are created and funded. If IAgentNft(nft).mint() reverts (e.g., due to internal logic, access control, or invalid URI), the entire transaction reverts. However, the token and LP have already been created and funded with applicationThreshold. The funds are now in the token contract, but the NFT is not minted, so the agent is not registered in the NFT contract. The proposer cannot withdraw because the application status is Executed, and the TBA and DAO are created. The funds are permanently locked in the token contract because there is no way to reclaim them — the NFT is the only access control mechanism for the agent. This is a critical state inconsistency: the protocol assumes that if the token is created, the NFT will be minted, but there is no atomicity. The financial impact is that any failure in NFT minting (even due to a bug in the NFT contract) results in permanent loss of applicationThreshold per failed agent.

vulnerabilities.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds Triggers Unintended Execution Path
vulnerabilities.description: The contract's withdraw() function transfers funds back to the proposer, but if an attacker sends funds directly to the contract address after a withdrawal is requested but before it is executed, those funds are incorrectly treated as new application deposits. This occurs because the contract has no mechanism to distinguish between user-initiated deposits (via proposeAgent or initFromBondingCurve) and system-generated returns (from withdraw()). The _executeApplication function then consumes these returned funds as if they were new application deposits, leading to double-spending of the same assetToken by the protocol.

vulnerabilities.title: State Inconsistency in Custom Token Application Execution Leads to Double Liquidity Provision and Fund Theft
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication and executeTokenApplication functions both call _executeApplication, which assumes the token balance at address(this) is equal to the initial application threshold. However, for custom token applications (initiated via initFromToken), the token balance at address(this) is the initialLP provided by the user, while the assetToken balance is still the applicationThreshold. When _executeApplication is called, it uses initialAmount (applicationThreshold) to calculate liquidity provision for the assetToken, but uses IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) for the custom token side. This mismatch causes the protocol to deposit applicationThreshold worth of assetToken into the LP while only depositing initialLP worth of the custom token. Since the LP ratio is determined by the actual balances, the protocol effectively creates an asymmetric LP where the custom token side is underfunded, allowing the proposer to withdraw the full custom token balance (initialLP) while only having contributed applicationThreshold of assetToken. This results in the protocol losing the difference between initialLP and applicationThreshold in assetToken value, which can be exploited by an attacker who provides a large initialLP with a small applicationThreshold.

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call in executeApplication Leads to Funds Lockup
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function commits state (setting application.status to Executed and zeroing withdrawableAmount) before executing external calls to create token, LP, veToken, DAO, NFT, and TBA. If any of these external calls revert (e.g., due to gas limits, contract initialization failure, or forked behavior), the application state is permanently marked as Executed, preventing withdrawal or re-execution, while funds are stuck in the factory contract. This violates the principle of 'check-effects-interact' and creates irreversible state corruption.

vulnerabilities.title: Fork Behavioral Divergence in IAgentToken.liquidityPools() and IAgentVeToken.stake()
vulnerabilities.description: The contract assumes IAgentToken(token).liquidityPools()[0] returns a valid LP address and that IAgentVeToken(veToken).stake(...) will successfully stake LP tokens. However, if the deployed token or veToken contracts are forks (e.g., from a modified Uniswap V2/V3 or Convex-style system), these functions may have been removed, renamed, or moved to separate contracts. For example, in many forks, liquidity pools are created via a factory contract, not exposed via a liquidityPools() array, and staking is handled by a separate reward distributor. This causes _executeApplication to revert silently at C2 or C7, leaving the application in Executed state with funds locked and no LP or veToken created.

vulnerabilities.title: Insufficient Validation of Token Supply Parameters in executeBondingCurveApplication
vulnerabilities.description: The executeBondingCurveApplication function constructs _tokenSupplyParams using totalSupply, lpSupply, and vault values without validating that lpSupply <= totalSupply or that vault is non-zero. If lpSupply > totalSupply, the vaultSupply becomes negative (underflow), which may cause the token implementation to behave unpredictably (e.g., minting negative tokens, reverting on overflow). This is a precision boundary issue: the format selection (abi.encode) assumes valid mathematical relationships, but no domain validation is performed.

vulnerabilities.title: TBA Creation Uses ChainID Without Validation, Leading to ABI Incompatibility
vulnerabilities.description: The TBA creation uses assembly to read chainid() and passes it to IERC6551Registry.createAccount. However, if the TBA implementation expects a different chain ID encoding (e.g., 32-byte vs 8-byte) or if the registry is a fork that uses a different signature (e.g., requires blockhash instead of chainid), the account creation may fail silently or create an invalid TBA. This is an interface definition compatibility issue: the contract assumes the registry follows EIP-6551 exactly, but forks may have modified the function signature or encoding.

vulnerabilities.title: Application Status Change Before External Calls Enables Double-Spend via Reentrancy
vulnerabilities.description: Although the noReentrant modifier is used, the application.status is changed to Executed before any external calls in _executeApplication. If any of the called contracts (e.g., token, DAO, or NFT) reenter the factory via a callback (e.g., onTransfer, onMint), and if the reentrant call triggers another executeApplication on the same ID, the status is already Executed and the function will revert. However, if the reentrant call triggers a different application, the withdrawableAmount has already been zeroed, but the assetToken has not yet been transferred to the new token. This creates a window where funds are deducted from the proposer but not fully allocated, enabling partial fund loss.

vulnerabilities.title: Default Delegatee Can Be Set to Zero Address, Leading to Unstakable veToken
vulnerabilities.description: The setDefaultDelegatee function allows setting defaultDelegatee to address(0). In _executeApplication, IAgentVeToken(veToken).stake(...) uses defaultDelegatee as the delegatee. If defaultDelegatee is zero, the veToken contract may reject the stake (e.g., if it enforces non-zero delegatee), causing the stake to revert. However, the application status is already Executed and the LP tokens are locked in the veToken contract. This results in permanent loss of staking functionality and potential loss of governance rights, with no way to recover the LP tokens.

vulnerabilities.title: Access Control Bypass in withdraw() Allows Pre-Mature Withdrawal of Application Funds
vulnerabilities.description: The withdraw() function allows the proposer to withdraw funds once block.number > proposalEndBlock, but proposalEndBlock is set to block.number during proposeAgent(), meaning the withdrawal condition is immediately satisfied. This allows the proposer to withdraw the application threshold immediately after proposing, before any governance or liquidity provisioning occurs. This violates the intended economic model where funds should be locked until governance approval or maturity, enabling immediate theft of the application threshold from the protocol's custody.

vulnerabilities.title: Unit Mismatch in _executeApplication() Causes Incorrect Liquidity Provisioning and Token Dilution
vulnerabilities.description: In _executeApplication(), when using a custom token (non-null _applicationToken[id]), the function calls addLiquidity with IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) as the token amount and initialAmount as the assetToken amount. However, IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) returns the raw balance of the custom token held by the factory, which may include tokens transferred via initFromToken() that were not intended as liquidity. The function assumes this balance equals the initialLP, but no validation or conversion occurs. This causes the Uniswap pair to be created with incorrect token:asset ratios, leading to severe price distortion, front-running opportunities, and dilution of LP token value for legitimate stakers. The mismatch propagates to veToken staking, where staked LP tokens are based on this corrupted liquidity pool.

vulnerabilities.title: Data Structure Desynchronization in allTokens and allTradingTokens Causes Incomplete Agent Enumeration and Governance Failure
vulnerabilities.description: The arrays allTokens and allTradingTokens are appended to during _createNewAgentVeToken() and _createNewAgentToken() respectively, but are never trimmed when applications are withdrawn or executed. If an application is withdrawn (status = Withdrawn), its associated veToken and token remain in these arrays. Subsequent calls to totalAgents() return inflated counts, and any governance or analytics system relying on these arrays will process invalid or non-existent agents. This desynchronization breaks the invariant that array length equals active agents. For example, if 100 applications are proposed and 90 are withdrawn, totalAgents() still returns 100, causing downstream systems to attempt operations on 90 non-existent agents, leading to revert failures or incorrect reward distributions.

vulnerabilities.title: Unverified External Interface Compatibility in _createPair() Risks ABI Mismatch with Uniswap V2 Factory
vulnerabilities.description: The _createPair() function assumes IUniswapV2Factory.createPair(address,address) returns a pair address, but does not verify the returned address is non-zero or that the pair was actually created. If the Uniswap V2 factory implementation is forked or modified (e.g., by a chain-specific fork like PancakeSwap or SushiSwap), the function may call a different interface (e.g., with additional parameters or different return semantics). This can cause silent failures where the pair is not created, but the function proceeds, leading to subsequent addLiquidity() calls reverting due to non-existent pair. This breaks the entire agent bootstrap process for custom tokens and can lock user funds in the factory contract with no recovery mechanism.

vulnerabilities.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds Triggers Unintended Liquidity Creation
vulnerabilities.description: The contract's fallback/receive function (implicit) allows any ETH or ERC-20 token transfer to be received without validation. When a user initiates a withdrawal (withdraw() function), funds are transferred back to the proposer. However, if an attacker sends additional tokens to the contract address after the withdrawal request but before the executeApplication() call, those tokens are incorrectly treated as part of the application's liquidity pool. This allows an attacker to force the creation of a liquidity pool with malicious tokens, effectively stealing the proposer's asset token allocation and corrupting the application state. The contract cannot distinguish between user-initiated deposits and system-returned or attacker-initiated transfers, leading to mixed fund sources and state corruption.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Pattern 1: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds

vulnerabilities.title: Double Funding via Partial Execution and Refund Accounting in Custom Token Applications
vulnerabilities.description: In the initFromToken() function, users deposit both assetToken (applicationThreshold) and custom token (initialLP). When executeTokenApplication() is called, _executeApplication() is invoked, which transfers the custom token to the newly created LP. However, the contract does not verify that the amount of custom token transferred to the LP matches the initialLP amount provided during initFromToken(). If the custom token has a transfer fee (e.g., 5% tax), the actual amount received by the contract is less than initialLP. The contract then uses the actual balance (reduced by tax) to create liquidity, but the proposer is not refunded the difference. Crucially, the applicationThreshold (assetToken) is still fully transferred and used for liquidity, while the custom token's shortfall is silently absorbed. This creates a double funding vulnerability: the proposer pays full applicationThreshold in assetToken, but receives liquidity based on a reduced custom token amount — meaning the protocol effectively steals the tax portion from the proposer's custom token without compensation. The gap between requested (initialLP) and actual received amount is not accounted for, violating the SWAP_INTERFACE_PATTERN and REFUND_ACCOUNTING principles.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Pattern 6: Incorrect Difference Handling in Partial Execution

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call Verification in Liquidity Creation
vulnerabilities.description: In _executeApplication(), the application status is immediately set to Executed (state commitment) before the external Uniswap addLiquidity() call is made. If the addLiquidity() call fails (e.g., due to slippage, insufficient liquidity, or malicious router behavior), the state remains as Executed, but the liquidity pool is not created. This means the proposer cannot withdraw (status is no longer Active), yet the application is not properly executed. The funds (assetToken and custom token) remain locked in the contract with no recovery mechanism. The contract commits state (status change, token mapping) before verifying the success of critical external operations, violating the State Commitment Before Operation Verification pattern. This allows attackers to trigger call failures (e.g., by manipulating price or front-running) to permanently lock funds.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Pattern 6: State Commitment Before Operation Verification

vulnerabilities.title: Missing Caller Verification in Token Transfer During Withdrawal
vulnerabilities.description: In the withdraw() function, after verifying the sender is the proposer or has WITHDRAW_ROLE, the contract transfers the withdrawableAmount (assetToken) and any custom token balance back to the proposer. However, if an attacker sends custom tokens to the contract address after the application is created but before withdrawal, those tokens are included in the balance and transferred to the proposer. Since the contract does not verify the origin of the custom token balance (i.e., whether it was deposited by the proposer or injected by an attacker), an attacker can flood the contract with malicious tokens and force the proposer to receive them during withdrawal. This constitutes an authorization bypass in funds destination determination: the proposer receives tokens they did not deposit, potentially triggering unintended behavior (e.g., phishing, token spam, or contract reentrancy via malicious token's onTransfer hook). The contract assumes all token balances belong to the application, but does not track source origin.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Pattern 8: Authorization Bypass in Funds Destination Determination

vulnerabilities.title: Access Control Bypass in executeApplication Allows Premature Execution and Fee Avoidance
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function allows any user with WITHDRAW_ROLE or proposer status to execute an application immediately after proposal, without enforcing the intended maturity duration. The application.proposalEndBlock is set to block.number during proposal, making it immediately executable. This enables users to bypass the intended staking maturity period, allowing them to execute applications and stake liquidity tokens without waiting for the maturityDuration. Since the veToken staking is triggered immediately upon execution, users can stake and begin earning rewards without the required lock-up period, effectively avoiding the economic design of the protocol. This is a critical access control failure because the state variable used to enforce timing (proposalEndBlock) is set to an immediately satisfied value and never updated, and no access control prevents premature execution.

vulnerabilities.title: Unit Mismatch in _createNewAgentVeToken Causes Incorrect veToken Staking and Reward Dilution
vulnerabilities.description: The _createNewAgentVeToken function passes the full balance of the LP token (from address(this)) to IAgentVeToken(stakingAsset).balanceOf(address(this)), but the veToken implementation expects the staked amount to be normalized to the total supply of the LP token. However, the LP token is created with a fixed supply (via _tokenSupplyParams) and the initial liquidity is added via addInitialLiquidity(address(this)), which does not mint new tokens — it only transfers existing assetToken to the LP pool. The LP token balance at address(this) is equal to the initial applicationThreshold (e.g., 10,000 assetToken), but the total supply of the LP token is set to lpSupply (e.g., 100,000). When IAgentVeToken.stake() is called with 10,000 LP tokens, it interprets this as 10% of total supply, but the veToken contract expects the staked amount to be in raw LP token units, not normalized. However, if the veToken implementation uses a normalized staking model (e.g., stakedAmount / totalSupply * totalVeTokenSupply), then passing raw units without normalization causes incorrect veToken minting. This leads to users receiving disproportionately low veToken balances, diluting rewards for all stakers. The call chain is: executeApplication → _executeApplication → _createNewAgentVeToken → IAgentVeToken(stakingAsset).balanceOf(address(this)) → IAgentVeToken.stake(). The stake() function receives raw LP units but expects normalized units (or vice versa), causing miscalculated veToken issuance.

vulnerabilities.title: Data Structure Desynchronization in allTokens and allDAOs Causes Incomplete Agent Enumeration and Reward Distribution Failure
vulnerabilities.description: The arrays allTokens and allDAOs are appended to during _createNewAgentVeToken and _createNewDAO, respectively. However, if an application is withdrawn (via withdraw()) or re-executed (via executeApplication), the corresponding veToken and DAO are not removed from these arrays. This leads to desynchronization: the arrays grow indefinitely with dead or withdrawn agents, while the actual active agents are tracked only by _applications. When a function like totalAgents() is called, it returns the length of allTokens, which includes all ever-created veTokens — even those that were withdrawn. This breaks any external system relying on totalAgents() to calculate total staked value or reward distribution. For example, if 100 agents are created and 80 are withdrawn, totalAgents() returns 100, but only 20 are active. A reward pool of 10,000 tokens distributed per totalAgents() would give 100 tokens per veToken, but only 20 are active — meaning 8,000 tokens are incorrectly distributed to inactive veTokens, starving active users. The mathematical proof: 10,000 tokens / 100 veTokens = 100 per veToken. But only 20 are active → 20 * 100 = 2,000 tokens distributed to active users, 8,000 lost to inactive. This is a critical data integrity failure.

vulnerabilities.title: Uninitialized _tokenAdmin Causes executeApplication to Revert and Lock Funds Permanently
vulnerabilities.description: The _executeApplication function requires _tokenAdmin != address(0) to proceed. However, _tokenAdmin is only set via setTokenAdmin(), which is only callable by DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. If the admin never calls setTokenAdmin(), then any call to executeApplication() will revert. This means that even if users pay the applicationThreshold (e.g., 10,000 assetToken), their funds are permanently locked in the contract because the execution path is blocked. The withdraw() function can only be called by the proposer, but it only returns the applicationThreshold — it does not release the LP token or veToken assets created during execution. Since execution never completes, the LP token is never created, and the assetToken remains in the contract. The funds are irrecoverable unless the admin sets _tokenAdmin. This is a critical design flaw: user funds are locked due to an unenforced initialization requirement. Mathematical proof: 100 users each pay 10,000 assetToken → 1,000,000 assetToken locked permanently if _tokenAdmin is not set.

vulnerabilities.title: Incorrect TBA Creation in executeApplication Leads to Unreachable Token-Bound Accounts and NFT Metadata Corruption
vulnerabilities.description: The TBA (Token Bound Account) is created using IERC6551Registry.createAccount() with the chainId, nft address, and virtualId. However, the virtualId is set to 0 in the Application struct during proposeAgent() and only updated in _executeApplication() after TBA creation. This means that when createAccount() is called, application.virtualId is still 0, so the TBA is created with virtualId=0. Later, the virtualId is updated to IAgentNft(nft).nextVirtualId(), but the TBA is already created with the wrong ID. This breaks the TBA-NFT linkage: the TBA is bound to virtualId=0, but the NFT is minted with virtualId=N (e.g., 100). Any external system querying the TBA for NFT metadata will fail, and the TBA will not be associated with the correct NFT. This is a representation boundary failure: the function expects virtualId to be set before TBA creation, but it is set after. The call chain: proposeAgent() → virtualId=0 → executeApplication() → createAccount(virtualId=0) → then virtualId=N. The TBA is permanently misbound.

vulnerabilities.title: State Inconsistency in executeApplication Allows Double-Withdrawal of Funds
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function sets application.withdrawableAmount to 0 and changes status to Executed before performing any external calls. However, the withdraw function only checks that the application status is Active and that the proposalEndBlock has passed. Since executeApplication does not revert on failure of any subcall, an attacker can trigger executeApplication, let one of the external calls fail (e.g., due to insufficient liquidity or reentrancy), and then call withdraw() again because the status remains Active in the event of a revert. This allows the proposer to withdraw the same applicationThreshold amount twice: once via executeApplication (which transfers funds to the token contract) and again via withdraw (which transfers the same amount back to the proposer). The state variable withdrawableAmount is reset to 0 only if executeApplication completes successfully, but if any subcall fails, the transaction reverts and the state remains unchanged — yet the assetToken has already been transferred to the token contract. This creates a scenario where the proposer loses the initial applicationThreshold to the token contract (as part of liquidity provision) but can still withdraw it again via withdraw(), effectively stealing the funds.

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call in executeApplication Allows Reentrancy and Fund Theft
vulnerabilities.description: The _executeApplication function commits state (sets application.status to Executed and zeroizes withdrawableAmount) before executing external calls to create tokens, LPs, DAOs, and stake liquidity. If any external call reverts (e.g., due to malicious token implementation or insufficient liquidity), the state remains permanently committed, preventing the application from being withdrawn or re-executed, while the user's assetToken (applicationThreshold) is permanently locked in the contract. This violates Pattern 7 (State Commitment Timing) and Pattern 6 (State Synchronization in Function Chains).

vulnerabilities.title: Missing User Protection in executeApplication and executeTokenApplication Allows Slippage and Fund Loss
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication and executeTokenApplication functions create liquidity pools and stake LP tokens without allowing the user to specify minimum acceptable output (e.g., minimum LP tokens or veToken received). This exposes users to front-running and MEV attacks where an attacker can manipulate the Uniswap V2 price by swapping assetToken before the user's transaction, causing the user to receive far less LP tokens than expected. Since the function uses 0 slippage tolerance (addLiquidity with 0, 0), users have no protection. This violates Pattern 1 (User Control Over Execution Outcomes).

vulnerabilities.title: Inconsistent Accounting in withdraw() When Custom Token Exists Leads to Double Withdrawal
vulnerabilities.description: In the withdraw() function, if a custom token exists (_applicationToken[id] != address(0)), the function transfers the entire balance of the custom token to the proposer. However, the initial application.withdrawableAmount (equal to applicationThreshold) is also transferred. This means the proposer receives both the original assetToken deposit AND the full balance of the custom token, even if the custom token was funded by the protocol or other users. This violates Pattern 3 (Execution Boundaries and Validation Consistency) because the accounting references the requested value (applicationThreshold) and the actual token balance inconsistently, leading to unauthorized fund transfer.

vulnerabilities.title: Unverified External Token Interface in isCompatibleToken() Enables Fake Token Exploitation
vulnerabilities.description: The isCompatibleToken() function uses try-catch to verify token compatibility, but only checks name(), symbol(), totalSupply(), and balanceOf(). An attacker can deploy a malicious ERC20 that returns arbitrary values (e.g., name='FakeToken', symbol='FAKE', totalSupply=1e18, balanceOf(address(this))=1e18) to bypass the check. The token may not implement required functions like approve() or transferFrom(), causing _executeApplication to revert during addLiquidity or forceApprove(), but the application is already marked as Active and the user's assetToken is locked. This violates Pattern 8 (External System Assumptions) and Pattern 2 (Validation Timing).

vulnerabilities.title: Uninitialized _uniswapRouter in _createPair() Causes Permanent Protocol Lockup
vulnerabilities.description: The _createPair() function assumes _uniswapRouter is set and calls IUniswapV2Router02(_uniswapRouter).factory(). If _uniswapRouter is not set (e.g., during early deployment or if admin forgets to set it), the call reverts. This causes _executeApplication to revert, but the application status is already set to Executed and withdrawableAmount is zeroed. The user cannot withdraw because status != Active, and the application cannot be re-executed. The assetToken deposit is permanently locked. This violates Pattern 6 (State Synchronization) and Pattern 7 (State Commitment Timing).

vulnerabilities.title: Default Delegatee Can Be Set to Malicious Address, Enabling veToken Reward Theft
vulnerabilities.description: The setDefaultDelegatee() function allows the admin to set defaultDelegatee, which is used in IAgentVeToken(veToken).stake(..., defaultDelegatee). If the admin sets defaultDelegatee to a malicious address, all newly staked veTokens will delegate voting power to that address. Since veToken represents voting power in the DAO, this allows the attacker to control governance of all newly created Agent DAOs. This violates Pattern 5 (Recipient Selection Logic) and Pattern 4 (Access Control in Interfaces) because the interface does not indicate that defaultDelegatee is a critical governance parameter.

vulnerabilities.title: Zero InitialLP in initFromToken() Not Checked Until After Transfer, Leading to Fund Lockup
vulnerabilities.description: In initFromToken(), the requirement 'require(initialLP > 0, "InitialLP must be greater than 0");' is checked after IERC20(tokenAddr).safeTransferFrom(sender, address(this), initialLP). If initialLP is 0, the transfer does nothing (as per SafeERC20), but the application is still created with a zero balance. Later, in _executeApplication, when adding liquidity, IERC20(tokenAddr).balanceOf(address(this)) is 0, so addLiquidity is called with 0, 0, creating a 0-liquidity pool. The user's assetToken deposit is locked, and the token cannot be used. This violates Pattern 2 (Validation Timing) and Pattern 3 (Execution Boundaries).

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call in executeApplication Leads to Funds Lockup
vulnerabilities.description: In the _executeApplication function, the application status is changed to Executed (state commitment) before the external calls to create the token, LP, veToken, DAO, NFT, and TBA are completed. If any of these external calls revert (e.g., due to gas limits, contract initialization failure, or malicious implementation), the application state is permanently marked as Executed, but the components are not created. This prevents the proposer from withdrawing the initial deposit (since status is no longer Active) and the funds remain locked in the factory contract indefinitely.

vulnerabilities.title: Token Application Mapping Allows Reuse of Token Address After Withdrawal, Enabling Double-Spend
vulnerabilities.description: The _tokenApplication mapping tracks which token address is associated with which application ID. However, in the withdraw function, when a custom token is withdrawn, _tokenApplication[customToken] is set to 0, but there is no check in initFromToken to ensure the token address has never been used before. An attacker can create an application with a token, withdraw it, then call initFromToken again with the same token address to create a new application. This allows the same token to be used for multiple virtual personas, enabling double-spending of the same underlying asset across multiple agents.
vulnerabilities.location: initFromToken(address, uint8[], bytes32, address, uint32, uint256, uint256)

vulnerabilities.title: Unbounded Gas Consumption in _createNewDAO and _createNewAgentToken During Initialization
vulnerabilities.description: The _createNewDAO and _createNewAgentToken functions use Clones.clone() to deploy new contracts, followed by an initialize() call. These are external calls that consume gas. The caller of executeApplication or initFromToken pays for all gas, but if the deployed contract's initialize() function has unbounded loops or expensive operations (e.g., iterating over large arrays, calling external contracts), the transaction can run out of gas after state changes (like incrementing _nextId and setting status to Executed) have already occurred. This results in partial execution: the application is marked as Executed, but the token/DAO is not created, locking funds permanently.
vulnerabilities.location: _createNewDAO(string memory, IVotes, uint32, uint256) and _createNewAgentToken(string memory, string memory, bytes memory)

vulnerabilities.title: Authorization Context Not Bound in executeApplication — Front-Running Risk
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function allows any address with WITHDRAW_ROLE or proposer status to execute an application. However, the authorization (proposer status) is not bound to the specific parameters of the application (e.g., token supply, DAO parameters). An attacker can observe a legitimate proposal, then front-run the executeApplication call with the same ID but different parameters (e.g., changing the defaultDelegatee or tokenSupplyParams via a maliciously modified contract), effectively hijacking the execution context. Since the function uses _tokenSupplyParams (a global variable) instead of the application's stored parameters, the attacker can influence the token creation logic.

vulnerabilities.title: Fork Behavioral Divergence in Uniswap V2 Router Integration
vulnerabilities.description: The contract assumes the Uniswap V2 Router's factory() returns a factory contract that supports createPair(token, assetToken). However, many forks (e.g., SushiSwap, PancakeSwap) have moved fee collection and liquidity management logic to separate distributor contracts. In such forks, calling createPair() may return a valid pair address, but fees generated from trading are not collected by the factory or routed to the AgentFactoryV4. This results in liquidity being added but fees accumulating in the fork's distributor contract, making them inaccessible to the agent ecosystem. The contract has no mechanism to detect or adapt to fork-specific behavior.

vulnerabilities.title: Mathematical Domain Violation in Liquidity Calculation via forceApprove and addLiquidity
vulnerabilities.description: The _executeApplication function calls IERC20(token).forceApprove(_uniswapRouter, type(uint256).max) and IERC20(assetToken).forceApprove(_uniswapRouter, initialAmount). If the token has a totalSupply of 0 (e.g., due to a buggy token implementation), then IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) returns 0. The addLiquidity call then passes (0, initialAmount) to the router. While Uniswap V2 allows zero liquidity for one side, this creates an asymmetric pool where the token has no liquidity and infinite price. This is mathematically invalid for any meaningful trading pair. The function does not validate that the token balance is greater than zero before proceeding, leading to a broken pool that cannot be traded on.

vulnerabilities.title: Precision Loss in Token Supply Parameters Encoding
vulnerabilities.description: The setTokenSupplyParams function encodes seven uint256 values into a single bytes parameter. When decoded in _createNewAgentToken, these values are interpreted as uint256. However, if the underlying token implementation expects these values to be interpreted as uint128 or uint64 (e.g., for gas efficiency), and the values exceed those bounds, silent truncation occurs. For example, if maxSupply is set to 2^130, it will be truncated to 0 when interpreted as uint128 in the token contract. The factory does not validate that the encoded values fit within the expected range of the target token contract, leading to silent precision loss and incorrect token economics.
vulnerabilities.location: setTokenSupplyParams(uint256, uint256, uint256, uint256, uint256, uint256, address) and _createNewAgentToken(string memory, string memory, bytes memory)

vulnerabilities.title: Inconsistent State Restoration in Withdraw Function for Custom Tokens
vulnerabilities.description: In the withdraw function, when a custom token is withdrawn, the code transfers the token balance to the proposer and clears _tokenApplication[customToken] and _applicationToken[id]. However, the token is still listed in allTradingTokens. This creates an inconsistency: the token is no longer associated with any application, but remains in the global list. If the token is later used in initFromToken, the check _tokenApplication[tokenAddr] == 0 passes (correctly), but the token is already in allTradingTokens, which may be used for auditing or UI display. This leads to misleading state representation and potential double-counting in analytics.

vulnerabilities.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds Triggers Unintended Investment Logic
vulnerabilities.description: The AgentFactoryV2 contract has a critical vulnerability where funds sent to the contract address (e.g., as a withdrawal refund or external transfer) are automatically processed by the executeApplication function when called by an attacker. This occurs because executeApplication uses the contract's own balance as the source of liquidity for creating new agent tokens and LP pools. An attacker can send funds to the contract address, then trigger executeApplication on a pending application, causing the contract to use those externally sent funds as if they were the proposer's locked application threshold. This results in the attacker gaining control of newly created tokens, veTokens, DAOs, and NFTs without having paid the application threshold, effectively stealing protocol assets.

vulnerabilities.title: Access Control Bypass in executeApplication Allows Unauthorized Token Creation and Fund Drain
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function allows any user with WITHDRAW_ROLE or who is the proposer to execute an application, but it does not verify that the application has been properly approved or that the proposer has not already withdrawn. This creates a boundary inconsistency where economic state (token creation, liquidity provision, veToken staking) is triggered by a non-governance actor. An attacker can repeatedly call executeApplication on the same application after withdrawing, draining the protocol's assetToken balance by creating multiple instances of the same agent token and LP pool. The state variable application.withdrawableAmount is reset to 0 upon execution, but the application.status is only checked at the start and not re-validated after withdrawal, allowing re-execution. This violates access control boundaries because economic state changes (token deployment, liquidity injection, veToken minting) should only be triggerable by governance or after a proper approval process, not by arbitrary users with withdraw rights.

vulnerabilities.title: Unit Mismatch in Liquidity Provision Causes Incorrect veToken Staking and Reward Dilution
vulnerabilities.description: In executeApplication, the function transfers initialAmount (equal to applicationThreshold) from the factory to the newly created agent token contract, then calls addInitialLiquidity(address(this)) on the token. The token contract then uses this amount to create an LP pair with assetToken. Later, IAgentVeToken(veToken).stake(IERC20(lp).balanceOf(address(this)), ...) is called, which stakes the entire LP token balance held by the factory. However, the factory never holds any LP tokens after addInitialLiquidity() — because addInitialLiquidity() is expected to transfer the assetToken to the LP and mint LP tokens to the token contract, not to the factory. The factory's LP balance is therefore 0, causing the stake() call to stake 0 LP tokens. This means the veToken is minted but not backed by any staked liquidity, breaking the economic model. The representation boundary is violated: executeApplication assumes that addInitialLiquidity() leaves LP tokens in the factory, but the IAgentToken interface (and standard Uniswap V2 pattern) expects LP tokens to be minted to the token contract. This unit mismatch propagates: the veToken is initialized with a staking asset (LP) but receives 0 staked amount, causing all future veToken rewards to be diluted to 0, and users who stake via this veToken receive no yield.
vulnerabilities.location: executeApplication(uint256 id, bool canStake) - lines 185-186 and 200

vulnerabilities.title: Desynchronized Collection Iteration in allTokens and allDAOs Causes Missing Agent Tracking and Governance Failure
vulnerabilities.description: The arrays allTokens and allDAOs are appended to during _createNewAgentToken and _createNewDAO, but never pruned when applications are withdrawn or executed. This creates a data structure boundary inconsistency: the arrays grow indefinitely, but the _applications mapping is the true source of truth. Functions like totalAgents() return the length of allTokens, which includes executed and withdrawn agents. This causes a desynchronization between the visible agent count and actual active agents. An attacker can exploit this by proposing and withdrawing 1000 applications without executing them. totalAgents() will return 1000, but only 0 are active. Any external system (dashboard, oracle, reward distributor) relying on totalAgents() will miscalculate total supply, reward distribution, or governance weight. For example, if a reward pool of 10,000 assetToken is distributed proportionally to totalAgents(), and 1000 fake agents are created, each real agent receives only 10 assetToken instead of 10,000. The mathematical proof: 10,000 / 1000 = 10 per agent, whereas correct distribution should be 10,000 / 1 = 10,000 per real agent. The financial impact: real users lose 99% of expected rewards, while the attacker gains no direct funds but causes systemic underpayment.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Data Access and Collection Integrity Violation
vulnerabilities.location: allTokens, allDAOs arrays and totalAgents() function

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call in executeApplication
vulnerabilities.description: In executeApplication, the application status is set to Executed (state commitment) before performing critical external calls to create token, DAO, veToken, NFT, TBA, and stake liquidity. If any of these external calls revert (e.g., due to gas limits, contract bugs, or malicious implementations), the application status remains Executed, but the Agent components are not created. This permanently locks the application in an inconsistent state: the withdrawableAmount has been consumed, the proposer cannot withdraw, and no Agent is created. The funds (applicationThreshold) are permanently trapped in the factory contract.

vulnerabilities.title: Insufficient Input Validation in _createNewAgentVeToken for Staking Asset
vulnerabilities.description: The _createNewAgentVeToken function accepts any address as stakingAsset without validating that it is a valid ERC20 token or that it has sufficient liquidity. When IAgentVeToken(veToken).stake(...) is called, it attempts to transfer the balance of the staking asset from the factory contract. If the stakingAsset is not a valid ERC20 token (e.g., a non-contract address, or a contract that reverts on transfer), the stake() call reverts. However, the veToken and other components are already created and committed. This results in a partially created Agent: the veToken exists but cannot be staked, rendering it useless. The proposer loses the applicationThreshold and gains no value.
vulnerabilities.location: _createNewAgentVeToken(string memory, string memory, address, address, bool)

vulnerabilities.title: Unbounded Array Growth in allTokens and allDAOs
vulnerabilities.description: The arrays allTokens and allDAOs are appended to without bound during every call to _createNewAgentToken and _createNewDAO. These arrays are used for enumeration (e.g., totalAgents() returns allTokens.length). As the number of deployed Agents grows, reading from these arrays becomes increasingly expensive in gas, eventually exceeding block gas limits. This makes the contract unusable for enumeration and can prevent legitimate users from interacting with the system. There is no mechanism to prune or cap these arrays.
vulnerabilities.location: allTokens, allDAOs arrays in storage; _createNewAgentToken, _createNewDAO functions

vulnerabilities.title: Missing Validation of TBA Implementation Address
vulnerabilities.description: The proposeAgent function accepts tbaImplementation as a user-provided address with no validation. In executeApplication, this address is used to create a Token Bound Account via IERC6551Registry(tbaRegistry).createAccount(...). If the tbaImplementation is not a valid TBA implementation (e.g., does not conform to ERC-6551 registry expectations, or is a malicious contract), the TBA creation may fail silently or create a non-functional account. Since the TBA is critical for future interactions (e.g., governance, access control), this results in a broken Agent with no recovery path. The proposer loses their applicationThreshold and gains no usable Agent.
vulnerabilities.location: proposeAgent(string memory, string memory, string memory, uint8[] memory, bytes32, address, uint32, uint256)

vulnerabilities.title: Insecure Use of Block Timestamp for Maturity Duration
vulnerabilities.description: The maturityDuration is added to block.timestamp in _createNewAgentVeToken to set the lock period. However, block.timestamp is manipulable by miners (within ~15 seconds). If an attacker deploys a malicious veToken implementation that checks the lock period and allows early unstaking if the timestamp is too far in the future, they could exploit this to withdraw staked assets prematurely. The factory contract assumes the lock period is secure, but the actual enforcement is delegated to an external contract that may not validate the timestamp properly. This creates a potential for fund theft if the veToken implementation is compromised or poorly designed.
vulnerabilities.location: _createNewAgentVeToken(string memory, string memory, address, address, bool)

vulnerabilities.title: Division by Zero in Validator Reward Distribution Due to Unchecked totalStaked
vulnerabilities.description: In _distributeValidatorRewards, the function calculates validator rewards using (amount * votes) / totalStaked, but totalStaked can be zero if no tokens are staked on a virtual persona despite the persona being eligible for rewards. This leads to a division by zero, causing the transaction to revert and preventing any validator rewards from being distributed for that virtualId. This breaks the reward distribution invariant and results in permanent loss of validator rewards for all validators associated with that virtualId. The issue arises because _prepareAgentsRewards only skips agents with staked amount below stakeThreshold, but does not validate that totalStaked > 0 before using it in division. Since totalStaked is a uint256 and can be zero (e.g., if nft.totalStaked(virtualId) returns 0 due to a bug in IAgentNft or if all staked tokens were withdrawn), the division fails catastrophically.

vulnerabilities.title: executeApplication Can Partially Fail, Leaving Funds Locked and State Inconsistent
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function performs multiple external calls to create token, LP pool, veToken, DAO, NFT, TBA, and stake liquidity. If any of these external calls fail after state has been modified (e.g., application.status set to Executed and withdrawableAmount zeroed), the user's initial asset token deposit (applicationThreshold) is permanently locked in the contract, and the application cannot be withdrawn. There is no rollback mechanism, and the user loses their funds with no recourse.

vulnerabilities.title: Application Status Updated Before External Calls, Enabling Permanent Fund Lock
vulnerabilities.description: In executeApplication, application.status is set to Executed and withdrawableAmount is zeroed BEFORE any external calls are made. If any subsequent external call (e.g., minting NFT, creating TBA, or staking) reverts, the application is permanently marked as Executed and the funds are irreversibly removed from the user's withdrawable balance. The user cannot withdraw because status != Active, and cannot re-execute because status == Executed. This creates a permanent denial-of-service and fund lock.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing User Protection Against Partial Execution in executeApplication
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function performs a sequence of 7 critical external operations to bootstrap a user's agent. The user has no mechanism to specify minimum acceptable outcomes (e.g., 'at least create token and LP'). If any step fails after the user's funds are consumed, they lose their entire applicationThreshold deposit with no recourse. No fallback, partial success handling, or user consent for partial execution is provided. This violates Pattern 1: user asset positions are reduced without any bounds or protection.

vulnerabilities.title: executeApplication Uses Stale State for Liquidity Pool Address
vulnerabilities.description: In executeApplication, the LP address is retrieved via IAgentToken(token).liquidityPools()[0] BEFORE the token's initialize() function has been called. The initialize() function for IAgentToken is called immediately after this line. The liquidityPools() array is likely empty or uninitialized at the time of access, causing the call to revert due to array index out of bounds. This results in a failed execution, locked funds, and inconsistent state — even though the token was successfully created.

vulnerabilities.title: Uninitialized _tokenAdmin Causes executeApplication to Revert, Locking Funds
vulnerabilities.description: The executeApplication function requires _tokenAdmin != address(0) before proceeding. However, _tokenAdmin is only set via setTokenAdmin(), which is only callable by DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. If the admin never calls setTokenAdmin(), executeApplication will revert on the first attempt. Since application.status is set to Executed and withdrawableAmount is zeroed BEFORE this check, any user who initiates execution while _tokenAdmin is zero will permanently lose their applicationThreshold deposit. This is a critical failure mode triggered by normal protocol usage if admin neglects setup.

vulnerabilities.title: executeApplication Zeroes withdrawableAmount Before Any Validation or External Call
vulnerabilities.description: The function zeroes application.withdrawableAmount immediately after the status check, before any validation (e.g., _tokenAdmin != address(0)) or external call. This means that if any subsequent check fails (e.g., token admin not set, TBA creation reverts, etc.), the user's funds are permanently removed from their withdrawable balance, and they cannot recover them. The accounting update (zeroing) occurs before any validation or execution, violating Pattern 2 and Pattern 3. This is a classic 'state change before validation' vulnerability.

vulnerabilities.title: executeApplication Uses Block.Timestamp + MaturityDuration for veToken Expiry, But MaturityDuration Is Set by Admin
vulnerabilities.description: The veToken expiry is set to block.timestamp + maturityDuration. However, maturityDuration is set by the admin via setMaturityDuration(). If the admin sets maturityDuration to 0 or a very small value, the veToken expires immediately. Users who stake their LP tokens for veToken receive no long-term benefits, and their staked assets are immediately unstakable. This is not a direct fund loss, but it breaks the economic model and can be exploited by a malicious admin to devalue user stakes. The admin has unchecked control over a core economic parameter.

vulnerabilities.title: TBA Creation Uses ChainID from Assembly, But NFT Address Is Hardcoded
vulnerabilities.description: The TBA creation uses assembly { chainId := chainid() } to get the chain ID, but the NFT contract address is hardcoded as 'nft'. If the NFT contract is deployed on a different chain than the AgentFactory, or if the TBARegistry expects a different chain ID (e.g., L2 vs L1), the TBA address will be incorrect. This breaks the Token Bound Account linkage, rendering the NFT metadata and governance permissions unusable. The protocol assumes chain consistency without verification, violating Pattern 8.

vulnerabilities.title: State Synchronization Failure in _distributeAgentRewards Leads to Validator Reward Underpayment
vulnerabilities.description: The function _distributeAgentRewards calculates validator rewards based on the total staked amount from the main reward, but does not ensure that the reward entry being processed is the most recent one for the given virtualId and mainRewardIndex. This allows a malicious actor to call distributeRewardsForAgents multiple times with the same mainRewardIndex and virtualId, causing the validator reward to be recalculated and redistributed multiple times, while the main reward's totalStaked remains unchanged. This results in validator rewards being paid out multiple times from the same pool of funds, diluting the reward for legitimate validators and potentially draining the protocol's reward pool.

vulnerabilities.title: Division by Zero in _distributeValidatorRewards Causes Reward Distribution Failure
vulnerabilities.description: In _distributeValidatorRewards, the function calculates validator rewards using the formula (amount * votes) / totalStaked. However, if totalStaked is zero (e.g., due to a bug in IAgentNft.totalStaked or if no tokens are staked), this results in a division by zero, causing the transaction to revert. This prevents any validator rewards from being distributed for that virtualId, even if validators have votes. Since the function does not check for zero totalStaked before division, this is a critical failure point that can be triggered by any agent with zero staked tokens, leading to permanent loss of validator rewards for all validators in that group.

vulnerabilities.title: Incorrect Reward Accounting in _distributeContributorRewards Due to Integer Division Truncation
vulnerabilities.description: In _distributeContributorRewards, the coreAmount is calculated as amount / coreTypes.length, which uses integer division. If amount is not evenly divisible by coreTypes.length, the remainder is lost. This lost amount is never accounted for in any other part of the system, resulting in permanent loss of protocol rewards. For example, if amount = 1000 and coreTypes.length = 3, coreAmount = 333, leaving 1 token unaccounted for. This error compounds over multiple reward distributions, leading to significant protocol insolvency over time.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing User Protection in claimAllRewards Allows Partial Execution and Fund Loss
vulnerabilities.description: The claimAllRewards function iterates over multiple virtualIds and contributionNftIds, calling _claimStakerRewards, _claimValidatorRewards, and _claimServiceRewards in sequence. If any of these subcalls revert (e.g., due to a zero division in _distributeValidatorRewards or an invalid NFT owner in _claimServiceRewards), the entire transaction reverts, but only after some claims have already been processed. This means users may receive partial rewards while others are lost, with no mechanism to specify minimum acceptable outcomes. Users cannot protect themselves from partial execution, and the protocol has no rollback mechanism for partially completed claims, leading to asymmetric loss of user funds.

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Settings Update Without Validation Allows Protocol Insolvency
vulnerabilities.description: The setRewardSettings function allows the governor to update reward shares (protocolShares, contributorShares, stakerShares, parentShares) without any bounds checking.
