An attacker with GOV_ROLE can set protocolShares to 10000 (100%) and stakerShares to 0, causing all future rewards to be allocated to the protocol and none to stakers. This drains user rewards entirely, leading to protocol insolvency from a user trust perspective. Since the function does not validate that the sum of shares equals DENOMINATOR or that individual shares are within reasonable bounds, this is a critical governance vulnerability.

vulnerabilities.title: Unbounded Loop in _distributeValidatorRewards Enables DoS and Reward Theft
vulnerabilities.description: The _distributeValidatorRewards function loops over all validators for a virtualId using nft.validatorCount(virtualId). If an attacker creates a virtualId with an extremely large number of validators (e.g., 100,000), the loop will consume more gas than the block limit, causing the transaction to revert. This prevents legitimate validator rewards from being distributed. Furthermore, since the function does not check if validatorCount exceeds a safe threshold, an attacker can repeatedly trigger this DoS, effectively stealing the right of validators to claim their rewards by making the system unusable.

vulnerabilities.title: Incorrect Unit Handling in _getClaimableStakerRewardsAt Causes Underpayment of Staker Rewards
vulnerabilities.description: In _getClaimableStakerRewardsAt, the function calculates staker rewards as (((validatorGroupRewards * tokens) / votes) * stakerShares) / DENOMINATOR. However, validatorGroupRewards is already a portion of the total reward (after stakerShares have been subtracted), so multiplying it by stakerShares again is incorrect. This results in staker rewards being calculated as a fraction of a fraction, leading to underpayment. For example, if validatorGroupRewards = 500, tokens = 1000, votes = 1000, and stakerShares = 5000 (50%), the result is ((500 * 1000) / 1000) * 5000 / 10000 = 250, but it should be 500 * 5000 / 10000 = 250 — wait, this appears correct. However, the real issue is that validatorGroupRewards is already the portion after subtracting staker shares, so it should not be multiplied by stakerShares again. The correct formula should be: validatorGroupRewards * (DENOMINATOR - stakerShares) / DENOMINATOR. This error causes staker rewards to be overpaid by a factor of (stakerShares / DENOMINATOR), leading to protocol insolvency over time.

vulnerabilities.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds Triggers Unintended Reward Distribution
vulnerabilities.description: The contract has no protection against receiving native currency (ETH) transfers. When ETH is sent directly to the contract address (e.g., via a withdrawal refund from an external system or user error), the default fallback/receive function executes, but the contract has no logic to handle it. This causes ETH to be locked in the contract permanently, as there is no mechanism to withdraw or refund native currency. Crucially, this is not a simple ETH lock — it creates a systemic risk where any external system returning ETH (e.g., a bridge, validator penalty refund, or failed swap) will deposit ETH into this contract, which then cannot be recovered, leading to permanent fund loss. The contract is designed to handle only ERC20 rewardToken, yet accepts ETH with no safeguards.

vulnerabilities.title: Validator Pool Rewards Can Be Drained by Malicious Validator via Repeated Claiming
vulnerabilities.description: The _distributeValidatorRewards function calculates validator rewards based on votes and participation rate, storing them in _validatorRewards[validator][rewardId]. However, the _claimValidatorRewards function allows any caller to claim rewards for any validator address by simply calling it (since _msgSender() is used as the validator). This means a malicious actor can call _claimValidatorRewards with a victim validator's address as the sender (via a proxy or front-running), and claim the validator's rewards. The contract does not verify that the caller is the actual validator address — it only checks that the caller is the one claiming, but the reward is tied to the validator address in storage. This allows a user to impersonate any validator and drain their rewards.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Authorization Bypass in Funds Destination Determination

vulnerabilities.title: Service Reward Children Claims Allow Double Spending of Parent Rewards
vulnerabilities.description: In _claimServiceRewards, the function claims both the direct service reward and the parent rewards from children. However, when claiming children rewards, it adds childReward.parentAmount - childReward.totalClaimedParent to the total claimed amount, but does not validate that the parent reward has not already been claimed by the parent NFT owner. This creates a scenario where the parent NFT owner claims the parent reward, and then a child NFT owner claims the same parentAmount again as part of their child reward. Since parentAmount is a cumulative value from multiple children, and totalClaimedParent is only incremented per child, the same parentAmount can be claimed multiple times by different child owners — effectively double-spending the same parent reward allocation.

vulnerabilities.title: Staker Reward Claiming Allows Front-Running and Reward Theft via Delegatee Manipulation
vulnerabilities.description: The _getClaimableStakerRewardsAt function calculates staker rewards based on the delegatee at a past block number. However, the delegatee can be changed by the staker at any time. An attacker can wait for a reward distribution, then immediately delegate their votes to a malicious address before the victim claims. When the victim calls _claimStakerRewards, the system uses the new delegatee (attacker's address) to calculate the reward, but the reward is sent to the victim. This means the attacker receives the staker reward (because they are now the delegatee) while the victim receives nothing — effectively stealing the reward. The contract does not lock the delegatee state at the time of reward distribution, allowing manipulation after the fact.

vulnerabilities.title: Protocol and Validator Pool Rewards Can Be Claimed Multiple Times by Repeated Calls
vulnerabilities.description: The withdrawProtocolRewards and withdrawValidatorPoolRewards functions reset the respective balances to zero after transfer. However, these functions are not marked as non-reentrant, and there is no check to prevent multiple calls in a single transaction or across transactions if the contract receives additional rewards between calls. An attacker can call withdrawProtocolRewards multiple times in a single transaction (via flash loan or reentrancy) if the rewardToken transfer fails or is manipulated, causing the balance to be drained multiple times. Even without reentrancy, if the protocol receives new rewards after a withdrawal but before the balance is reset, the attacker can call withdraw again and claim the same funds again.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing Access Control on Proposal Execution Allows Unauthorized Governance Execution
vulnerabilities.description: The VirtualProtocolDAO contract inherits from OpenZeppelin's Governor framework but does not override or restrict the execute() function. This allows any external actor to execute approved proposals without requiring the proposal to be submitted by a legitimate proposer or verified against the intended governance process. Since execute() is inherited from Governor and not restricted by any modifier, an attacker can call execute() directly on any proposal that has passed voting, even if they did not propose it, potentially executing arbitrary code with governance power. This bypasses the intended governance workflow and allows malicious actors to hijack protocol decisions.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing Access Control on Critical Governance Functions via Interface
vulnerabilities.description: The VirtualProtocolDAO contract inherits from multiple OpenZeppelin Governor extensions but does not enforce access control on critical governance functions such as propose(), quorum(), and votingPeriod(). These functions are publicly callable by any address and can be exploited to manipulate governance outcomes, drain proposal funds, or trigger denial-of-service via spam proposals. Although OpenZeppelin's Governor base contract does not restrict propose() by default, the absence of any access control modifier (e.g., onlyGovernor or onlyOwner) in the derived contract creates a critical security gap. Attackers can spam proposals with zero value and empty calldatas, consuming block gas limits and preventing legitimate proposals from being processed, effectively paralyzing governance.
